items.stem: Which criterion assesses focus and organisation in Paper 1?
items.answer: Criterion C
items.markingKey: A. C is Focus and organisation.

items.stem: Explain why organising by aspect can be better than by device.
items.answer: Organising by aspect (e.g. how the text creates urgency) groups devices by effect, creating an argument rather than a catalogue.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Organising by aspect (e.g. how the text creates urgency) groups devices by effect, creating an argument rather than a catalogue. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Criterion C rewards length: the more paragraphs, the better." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Criterion C rewards coherent, focused development; a shorter, well-organised analysis can score higher than a long, repetitive one.
items.markingKey: Criterion C rewards coherent, focused development; a shorter, well-organised analysis can score higher than a long, repetitive one. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following post by a fitness influencer on a photo-sharing platform.

5 a.m. Rain. Didn't want to. Did it anyway. [flexed-biceps emoji]
Here's the thing nobody tells you: motivation is a myth. Discipline is a decision.
Link in bio for my 30-day reset plan (only 40 spots left!!)
#grindseason #nooffdays #mindset – 214k likes

Guiding question: How does the influencer construct an online persona to persuade followers?
Write the conclusion of a Paper 1 analysis that synthesises your argument and evaluates the text's overall effect.
items.answer: Thesis: the post presents authenticity as a product. (1) Fragments perform effort. (2) The antithesis slogan. (3) The scarcity appeal and hashtags turn the persona into marketing. Evaluation: "no off days" may promote unhealthy attitudes.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Thesis: the post presents authenticity as a product. (1) Fragments perform effort. (2) The antithesis slogan. (3) The scarcity appeal and hashtags turn the persona into marketing. Evaluation: "no off days" may promote unhealthy attitudes. Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: Write a transition sentence linking a paragraph on an advert's image to a paragraph on its slogan.
items.answer: Example: "If the image creates the feeling of belonging, the slogan names it, anchoring the picture's warmth to the brand."
items.markingKey: Example: "If the image creates the feeling of belonging, the slogan names it, anchoring the picture's warmth to the brand."

items.stem:
Read the following home-front poster from a fictional wartime nation, written in the style of 1940s propaganda.

[Image: a woman in overalls rolls up her sleeve beside a factory gate; behind her, the silhouettes of marching soldiers.]
THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT.
YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE.
Every shell you make is a letter home.
Don't let them down – report for factory work today.

Guiding question: How does the poster persuade women to take up factory work?
Outline a well-organised response, explaining how each section develops the line of argument (criterion C).
items.answer: Thesis: the poster recruits by equating industrial labour with the soldier's heroism and with love. (1) Parallel capitals equate front and lathe. (2) The metaphor "a letter home" transforms shells into affection. (3) The image of the rolled sleeve models readiness, and the imperative uses guilt. Evaluation: the empowerment is conditional – it serves the war effort rather than women's equality.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Thesis: the poster recruits by equating industrial labour with the soldier's heroism and with love. (1) Parallel capitals equate front and lathe. (2) The metaphor "a letter home" transforms shells into affection. (3) The image of the rolled sleeve models readiness, and the imperative uses guilt. Evaluation: the empowerment is conditional – it serves the war effort rather than women's equality. Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Organisation matters more to the reader than analysis."
items.answer: Organisation makes analysis visible; it is a means to communicate insight, not a substitute.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: a disorganised analysis obscures insight; clarity guides the examiner. Arguments against: organisation is only one of four criteria; insight is rewarded under A and B. Supported judgement: Organisation makes analysis visible; it is a means to communicate insight, not a substitute.

items.stem: Write a full plan and conclusion for a Paper 1 analysis of a text you have studied, showing how each paragraph builds the argument.
items.answer: Indicative content: thesis; paragraph topics with transitions; synthesising conclusion with evaluation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: thesis; paragraph topics with transitions; synthesising conclusion with evaluation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "evaluation"?
options: Judging how effectively a writer's choices achieve their purpose, or their implications
Evaluating one's own work against the assessment criteria to identify improvements
Paper 1 criterion "Focus and organisation" (5 marks): coherence, focus and development of the analysis
A word or phrase that links paragraphs and signals the relationship between ideas
items.answer: Judging how effectively a writer's choices achieve their purpose, or their implications
items.markingKey: A. "evaluation" is judging how effectively a writer's choices achieve their purpose, or their implications.

items.stem: Explain why focusing on fewer features in more depth earns more credit.
items.answer: Depth allows close analysis of language, connotation and effect, which criterion B rewards over a superficial list.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Depth allows close analysis of language, connotation and effect, which criterion B rewards over a superficial list. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Evaluation means saying whether you liked the text." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Evaluation judges the effectiveness and implications of the writer's choices for an audience and purpose, not personal taste.
items.markingKey: Evaluation judges the effectiveness and implications of the writer's choices for an audience and purpose, not personal taste. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following post from a travel blog written by a young backpacker in Vietnam.

Day 12. Hanoi. Honestly? I came for the Instagram shots – the lanterns, the train street, the egg coffee. What I got was Mrs Lan, who runs a tiny noodle stall and refused to let me pay because I tried (badly) to say 'thank you' in Vietnamese. Lesson learned: the best stuff here isn't on any list. #slowtravel

Write a criterion B-focused paragraph on "the best stuff here", analysing its effect and evaluating its success.
items.answer: Colloquialism: "the best stuff here" – informal diction creates a chatty, peer-to-peer voice.
items.markingKey: Colloquialism: "the best stuff here" – informal diction creates a chatty, peer-to-peer voice. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following pair of headlines and opening lines from two newspapers reporting the same student protest.

Newspaper A: 'Thousands of students march for affordable housing' – Students filled the city centre on Saturday, chanting and carrying handmade banners, to demand rent controls.
Newspaper B: 'Student mob brings city centre to standstill' – Shoppers were left stranded on Saturday as crowds of students blocked roads, causing chaos for local businesses.

Write a criterion B-focused paragraph on "Student mob", analysing its effect and evaluating its success.
items.answer: Loaded noun: "Student mob" – "mob" connotes violence and irrationality, delegitimising the protesters.
items.markingKey: Loaded noun: "Student mob" – "mob" connotes violence and irrationality, delegitimising the protesters. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Students should always criticise a non-literary text in Paper 1 to show evaluation."
items.answer: Evaluation should be balanced and evidence-based; it may praise, criticise or both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: criticism shows independence; many texts manipulate. Arguments against: evaluation can affirm effectiveness; forced criticism is unconvincing. Supported judgement: Evaluation should be balanced and evidence-based; it may praise, criticise or both.

items.stem: Write one analytical paragraph on a non-literary text you have studied that both analyses and evaluates a single authorial choice.
items.answer: Indicative content: choice identified with quotation; analysis of effect; evaluation of effectiveness and limitations.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: choice identified with quotation; analysis of effect; evaluation of effectiveness and limitations.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Paper 1 criterion "Language" (5 marks): clarity, variety and accuracy of language and appropriateness of register and style"?
items.answer: criterion D
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of criterion D.

items.stem: Explain the difference between formal register and informal register.
items.answer: Formal register uses complete sentences, precise vocabulary and impersonal constructions; informal register uses contractions, slang and conversational tone – unsuitable for analysis.
items.markingKey: Formal register uses complete sentences, precise vocabulary and impersonal constructions; informal register uses contractions, slang and conversational tone – unsuitable for analysis. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Using long, complicated words always earns marks for language." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Criterion D rewards clarity, precision and appropriateness; inflated vocabulary that obscures meaning can lower the mark.
items.markingKey: Criterion D rewards clarity, precision and appropriateness; inflated vocabulary that obscures meaning can lower the mark. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Replace the weak verb in: "The image shows that the bottle is important."
items.answer: Example: "The image foregrounds the bottle, isolating it against the grey crowd." (foregrounds/isolates/emphasises)

Using precise terminology, write two sentences on the effect of "Honestly?".
items.answer: Rhetorical question: "Honestly?" – the one-word question mimics speech and signals a confession to the reader.

items.answer: All criteria are equally weighted; clear language is the vehicle for every other criterion.

items.stem: Define the term "academic register".
items.answer: Formal, precise language suited to analytical writing
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: formal, precise language suited to analytical writing. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Evaluating one's own work against the assessment criteria to identify improvements"?
items.answer: self-assessment

items.answer: The best-fit approach allows occasional errors in an excellent response; top bands require control, not perfection.

items.stem: Explain the difference between summative assessment and formative assessment.
items.answer: Summative assessment measures achievement at the end (an exam mark); formative assessment, such as self-assessment, gives feedback to improve learning.

items.stem: A student's Paper 1 response analyses effects precisely but uses informal phrases such as "kind of" and "loads". Which criterion is affected and how could it improve?
items.answer: Criterion D (language); replace informal phrases with precise academic vocabulary and hedged verbs.

items.stem:
Read the following pair of headlines and opening lines from two newspapers reporting the same student protest.

Newspaper A: 'Thousands of students march for affordable housing' – Students filled the city centre on Saturday, chanting and carrying handmade banners, to demand rent controls.
Newspaper B: 'Student mob brings city centre to standstill' – Shoppers were left stranded on Saturday as crowds of students blocked roads, causing chaos for local businesses.

Guiding question: How do the two newspapers shape readers' opinions of the same event?
List what a top-band response (criteria A and B) would need to include for this text.
items.answer: Thesis: the same facts are framed as civic action (A) and disruption (B). (1) Diction: "march" versus "mob". (2) Whose perspective is centred. (3) A includes the demand; B omits it. Evaluation: neither is strictly false; framing operates through selection and connotation.
items.markingKey: Thesis: the same facts are framed as civic action (A) and disruption (B). (1) Diction: "march" versus "mob". (2) Whose perspective is centred. (3) A includes the demand; B omits it. Evaluation: neither is strictly false; framing operates through selection and connotation. Paper 1 criteria (5 marks each, 20 total). A Understanding and interpretation: grasp of the literal and implied meaning, references well chosen. B Analysis and evaluation: how textual features and authorial choices shape meaning, with evaluation of their effect. C Focus and organisation: a clear line of argument that answers the guiding question (or a chosen focus) and is developed coherently. D Language: clear, precise, varied academic register and accurate terminology. 5 = excellent, 3 = adequate, 1 = minimal.

items.stem: Write a short exemplar paragraph that would reach the top band for criterion B on a text you have studied, then annotate it to show why it meets the descriptors.
items.answer: Indicative content: perceptive analysis of specific choices; evaluation; annotations linked to descriptors.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: perceptive analysis of specific choices; evaluation; annotations linked to descriptors.

items.stem: Briefly explain why studying marked exemplars helps students improve.
items.answer: Exemplars show what each band looks like in practice, making abstract descriptors concrete and showing the gap between current and target performance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Exemplars show what each band looks like in practice, making abstract descriptors concrete and showing the gap between current and target performance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

Paper 1 criterion "Focus and organisation" (5 marks): coherence, focus and development of the analysis
A deliberate decision by the writer about language, structure, style or form
The final section that synthesises the argument and evaluates the text's overall effect, without merely repeating

items.answer: Precise verbs and terms (e.g. "undermines", "anchors") express exactly how a feature works, which also strengthens criterion B.

items.stem: Distinguish between a thematic structure and a sequential structure.
items.answer: A sequential structure follows the text from beginning to end; a thematic structure organises paragraphs around aspects of the argument. Thematic structures usually show focus more clearly.

Read the following post from a travel blog written by a young backpacker in Vietnam.

Day 12. Hanoi. Honestly? I came for the Instagram shots – the lanterns, the train street, the egg coffee. What I got was Mrs Lan, who runs a tiny noodle stall and refused to let me pay because I tried (badly) to say 'thank you' in Vietnamese. Lesson learned: the best stuff here isn't on any list. #slowtravel

Write one precise, academic sentence analysing "the lanterns, the train street, the egg coffee", using an exact analytical verb.
items.answer: Tricolon: "the lanterns, the train street, the egg coffee" – the list of clichéd photo spots satirises the tourist checklist.
items.markingKey: Tricolon: "the lanterns, the train street, the egg coffee" – the list of clichéd photo spots satirises the tourist checklist. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a city mayor at the opening of a public library in a multilingual neighbourhood.

Friends, neighbours – bienvenidos, karibu, welcome. Some people say libraries are relics, that everything we need is on our phones. But a phone cannot hold a child's hand through her first chapter book. A phone does not stay open late for the night-shift nurse who wants to finish her degree. This building belongs to you: to every language spoken on these streets, and to every language not yet learned.

Guiding question: How does the mayor construct the library as a place of belonging?
A student's thesis is: "The text uses many techniques to persuade." Assess it against criterion C and rewrite it to reach the top band.
items.answer: Thesis: the mayor presents the library as a human, multilingual home rather than a store of information. (1) Code-switching in the greeting includes migrant communities. (2) Anaphora and personification contrast the phone's limits with human care (the child, the nurse). (3) The final possessive "belongs to you" transfers ownership to residents. Evaluation: the speech is inclusive but sentimental; it avoids questions of funding.
items.markingKey: Thesis: the mayor presents the library as a human, multilingual home rather than a store of information. (1) Code-switching in the greeting includes migrant communities. Evaluation: the speech is inclusive but sentimental; it avoids questions of funding. Paper 1 criteria (5 marks each, 20 total). A Understanding and interpretation: grasp of the literal and implied meaning, references well chosen. B Analysis and evaluation: how textual features and authorial choices shape meaning, with evaluation of their effect. C Focus and organisation: a clear line of argument that answers the guiding question (or a chosen focus) and is developed coherently. D Language: clear, precise, varied academic register and accurate terminology. 5 = excellent, 3 = adequate, 1 = minimal.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Organisation matters more to the reader than analysis."
items.answer: Organisation makes analysis visible; it is a means to communicate insight, not a substitute.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: a disorganised analysis obscures insight; clarity guides the examiner. Arguments against: organisation is only one of four criteria; insight is rewarded under A and B. Supported judgement: Organisation makes analysis visible; it is a means to communicate insight, not a substitute.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column on art and artificial intelligence.

Last week a machine won a regional art prize. The judges, to their credit, were embarrassed. The machine, to its credit, was not – it cannot be embarrassed, which is precisely the point. Art has never been about the finished picture alone; it is about a person risking something in public. An algorithm risks nothing. It cannot fail, so it cannot really succeed.

Evaluate the text's effectiveness for its intended audience, considering how a different reader might respond.
items.answer: An artist may welcome the defence of human creativity; a technologist may argue the column ignores the human who prompts and curates.
items.markingKey: An artist may welcome the defence of human creativity; a technologist may argue the column ignores the human who prompts and curates. Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Criterion D is the least important of the Paper 1 criteria."
items.answer: All criteria are equally weighted; clear language is the vehicle for every other criterion.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it has the same marks as the others; content seems more important. Arguments against: language carries the analysis; poor expression obscures insight.
